About: the rotation curve of the Galaxy, vc2 = GM(s)/s, and the mass it needs beyond the light

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the disc of the Galaxy face-on out to 40 kpc, turning clockwise, with the glow of the stars and gas, the dashed solar circle s0 = 8.2 kpc with the Sun, seven filled tracers at 5 to 35 kpc moving at the model speed and a hollow ghost for each moving at the speed of the stars and gas alone, the dark halo glow and its dotted cut-off circle when included, the thin probe circle and a 10 kpc scale bar. Right: vc against s, with the dashed curve for the stars and gas alone, fixed points shaped like a measured flat curve (labelled “as observed”; they are the model with the halo to 40 kpc, not real data), the solid model curve, shading between solid and dashed when the halo is included, and a marker at the probe radius.
Controls
Dark halo: none or included. Cut-off radius: where the halo mass stops growing, 10 to 40 kpc. Changing either returns every tracer and ghost to the common line with t = 0. Probe radius s: moves only the probe circle, its marker and the readouts. Play runs the clock at 10.85 Myr per screen second.
Measured
Stars and gas: a Plummer sphere of 6 × 1010 M⊙ with b = 3 kpc. Halo: an NFW profile with rs = 20 kpc, its mass frozen beyond the cut-off. vc = √(vstars2 + vhalo2); M(s) = s vc2/G; orbits turned = vc t/(2π s).
Readouts
In the sidebar under Controls: the clock; s, vc and vstars+gas at the probe radius; M(s), the stars and gas inside s and the dark share 1 − Mstars+gas/M(s); and the orbits turned by the Sun and by the 35 kpc tracer and its ghost.
Conditions
Every orbit is a circle and all the mass is treated as spherical, so vc2 = GM(s)/s holds exactly; for a real flattened disc the enclosed mass differs by 10 to 20 per cent. The halo cut-off is a teaching device: real halos thin out gradually. The Milky Way’s own curve, from 21-cm gas and stellar velocities, stays near 220 to 240 km/s to at least 20 kpc.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Speed without a halo

Choose no dark halo, keep the cut-off at 40 kpc and set the probe radius to s = 10 kpc, where the readout gives the circular speed. Before moving the probe out to 40 kpc, predict the circular speed there.

2 · Mass without a halo

Keep no dark halo and move the probe back to s = 10 kpc, noting the enclosed mass M(s). Before moving the probe out to 40 kpc again, predict how M(s) changes.

3 · The tracer and its ghost

Now include the dark halo, keep the cut-off at 40 kpc and set the probe to s0 = 8.2 kpc. Before pressing play for one orbit of the Sun, predict how the tracer at 35 kpc moves compared with its ghost, which goes round at the speed the stars and gas alone would give.

4 · Mass with the halo

Keep the halo included with the cut-off at 40 kpc and set the probe radius to s = 10 kpc, noting M(s) and the mass of stars and gas inside s. Before moving the probe to 20 kpc and then to 40 kpc, predict how M(s) changes.

5 · Cutting the halo short

Keep the halo included with the cut-off at 40 kpc and set the probe radius to 30 kpc. Before moving the cut-off radius in to 15 kpc, predict what the solid curve does beyond 15 kpc.

6 · What the flat curve tells us

With the stars and gas alone, the circular speed falls beyond the bright disc, as the planets’ speeds do. The Galaxy’s measured curve instead stays near 230 km/s as far out as it is measured, at least 20 kpc, and the model with the halo keeps it flat out to 40 kpc, so M(s) = svc2/G keeps growing in proportion to s where the light has stopped.

Inside 40 kpc nearly nine tenths of the mass is then dark: a halo that must reach at least as far as the curve is measured flat. (The model treats the mass as spherical; a flat disc shifts these numbers by 10 to 20 per cent, not the conclusion.)

01

At a glance

A star on a circular orbit feels the pull of the mass inside its radius. This sim follows tracer stars round a model Milky Way and plots circular speed against radius, with and without an invisible dark halo.

What you'll learn

  • How the circular speed depends on the mass inside the orbit.
  • How the mass inside a radius is read off a rotation curve.
  • What the dark halo adds, and where.
  • What a cut-off in the halo does to the curve.
The opening view, face-on: tracers and ghosts start on one line.

What's on screen

  • Orange glow: the stars and gas, turning clockwise. Dashed circle: the Sun's orbit, s0 = 8.2 kpc.
  • Cyan tracers move at the model speed vc.
  • Hollow amber ghosts move at the speed the stars and gas alone would give.
  • Thin ring: the probe radius s.
  • Violet glow and dotted ring: the dark halo and its cut-off, when included.
  • Inset: vc against s. Solid: the model. Dashed: stars and gas alone. Grey dots, "as observed (illustrative)": the model with the halo, not data.
See itLook at the opening state. Watch for: the ghost circles sitting exactly under the tracers, with the clock at 0 Myr and the sim paused.

03

Without a halo, the speed falls as the mass runs out

A star on a circular orbit of radius s is held there by the mass M(s) inside it, for a spherical distribution. Setting vc²/s equal to GM(s)/s² gives the notes' eq. (7.14), restated as (9.13):

Eqs. (7.14) and (9.13). M(s) is the mass inside radius s.

With no halo, only the 6 × 1010 M⊙ of stars and gas pull. About 88% of it lies inside 10 kpc, so out to 40 kpc, M(s) grows only from 5.27 to 5.95 × 1010 M⊙, a rise of 13%, while s grows fourfold. So vc falls from 151 to 80 km/s, close to the s−1/2 law of a point mass.

Circular speed from the stars and gas alone: 151 km/s at 10 kpc, 80 km/s at 40 kpc.
Key idea. Where M(s) stops growing, vc = √(GM/s) falls as s−1/2.
See itSwitch the halo off and slide the probe from 10 kpc out to 40 kpc. Watch for: vc dropping from 151 to 80 km/s while M(s) rises only from 5.27 to about 5.95 × 1010 M⊙.
04

A flat curve needs mass that grows in proportion to s

Include the halo, cut off at 40 kpc, and the model vc stays between 229 and 233 km/s from 5 to 40 kpc. By (7.14), M(s) = s vc²/G must then grow in proportion to s: it roughly doubles each time the radius doubles.

Mass inside s with the halo included, cut off at 40 kpc.

Stars and gas add only 5.27, 5.80 and 5.95 × 1010 M⊙ inside those radii, so the dark share is 58%, 77% and 88%. For a spherical halo, the notes' eq. (7.15) gives the density that keeps vc flat:

Eq. (7.15). The density falls as 1/s².
s

This slider moves the sim's probe too. The halo and cut-off come from the sim's own controls.

See itInclude the halo, cut off at 40 kpc, and slide the probe from 10 kpc out to 40 kpc. Watch for: M(s) climbing from 1.25 to 4.94 × 1011 M⊙, and the dark share from 58% to 88%, while vc stays near 232 km/s.
05

Further out, the halo supplies more of the pull

A tracer and its ghost leave the start line together. After a time t each has turned v t/(2πs) of an orbit, the tracer at vc, the ghost at the speed of the stars and gas alone. The speeds differ by the mass ratio:

  • vc / vstars+gas = √(M(s) / Mstars+gas(s)).
  • At 5 kpc the dark share is 38%, the speeds are 229 and 180 km/s, and the ratio is 1.27.
  • At 35 kpc the dark share is 86%, the speeds are 232 and 85 km/s, and the ratio is 2.7.

One orbit of the Sun takes 217 Myr, about 20 s on screen at 1×. In that time the 35 kpc tracer has turned 0.23 of an orbit and its ghost only 0.09.

Key idea. The tracer is not dragged back. More mass inside needs more speed to stay on a circle.
See itInclude the halo, cut off at 40 kpc, and play the clock until the Sun is half way round. Watch for: the 35 kpc tracer pulling ahead of its ghost: after about 10 s, 0.12 of an orbit against 0.04.
06

A halo cut off short makes the curve fall again

The cut-off sets where the halo mass stops growing. Beyond it M(s) is fixed, so vc falls again as s−1/2: from 165 km/s at 30 kpc to 143 km/s at 40 kpc, a ratio of 0.87, and √(30/40) = 0.87.

Halo cut off at 15 kpc: the solid curve falls beyond it, but stays above the dashed one.

With the cut-off at 15 kpc, vc is still 232 km/s at 15 kpc, 202 at 20 kpc and 165 at 30 kpc, against 92 km/s for the stars and gas alone. The curve stays above the dashed one because the inner halo still lies inside the orbit. A curve measured flat out to 40 kpc therefore means the halo reaches at least that far.

See itInclude the halo, cut it off at 15 kpc, and put the probe at 30 kpc. Watch for: vc at 165 km/s, well below 232, yet above the 92 km/s of the stars and gas.
07

Where it matters

  • The Milky Way. The notes' Fig. 88 sets the measured curve against the one expected if mass followed light. At s0 ≈ 8.2 kpc the notes give v0 ≈ 230 km/s and M ≈ 1011 M⊙; the sim with the halo reads 232 km/s and 1.03 × 1011 M⊙.
  • Other spirals. In nearly every one measured far enough out, the curve rises and then stays nearly flat. The mass-to-light ratio inside s grows from a few to a few tens (notes, 9.2).
  • The whole Galaxy. Satellites and distant halo stars suggest a total of about 1012 M⊙. The sim's 4.9 × 1011 M⊙ inside 40 kpc is not that total.
Go deeper: a 1/s² halo cannot go on for ever

A density ρ ∝ 1/s² gives M(s) ∝ s, which never stops growing, so the total mass would be infinite: a real halo must fall off faster somewhere. The sim's cut-off is a teaching device for that. Also, vc² = GM/s is exact only for a spherical distribution; a real disc differs by 10 to 20%.

08

Summary

In one line. A star on a circular orbit is held by the mass inside its radius, so how speed changes with radius shows how that mass is spread out.
  • M(s) = s vc²/G (eq. 7.14, 9.13).
  • Stars and gas alone: vc falls from 151 to 80 km/s between 10 and 40 kpc.
  • A flat vc needs M(s) ∝ s and ρ ∝ 1/s² (eq. 7.15). The dark share rises from 38% at 5 kpc to 88% at 40 kpc.
  • A halo cut off at sc lets the curve fall again beyond it.

Common mix-ups

  • "A flat curve means the mass is spread evenly." It means M(s) ∝ s; the density falls as 1/s².
  • "The halo matters as much near the Sun as far out." The dark share is 38% at 5 kpc, 86% at 35 kpc.
  • "Once the light runs out, the curve must fall." Only if the mass runs out too: with the halo on, vc is 230 km/s at 40 kpc.

Things to try on your own

  • Include the halo, probe at s0 = 8.2 kpc: the dark share should read 52%.
  • Cut-off 25 kpc, probe 40 kpc: vc should read 184 km/s.
